breakfast.name: Marmite on Toast (Kiwi Marmite)
ingredients: Kiwi Marmite (NOT British Marmite — different yeast extract formula)
instructions: Toast bread until golden
Spread butter generously — must melt into the toast
Spread a thin layer of Kiwi Marmite over the butter
Kiwi Marmite is darker, slightly sweeter, and less bitter than British Marmite
The Marmite shortage of 2012 (after Christchurch earthquake damaged the factory) caused national panic
'Marmageddon' — New Zealanders panic-bought Kiwi Marmite when supplies ran out
This is a profoundly different product from British Marmite despite the similar name
New Zealanders feel very strongly about this distinction
The thin scraping is important — too much is overwhelming
breakfast.description: New Zealand's iconic breakfast — Kiwi Marmite (a distinctly different formula from British Marmite, darker and slightly sweeter) spread thinly on buttered toast. The 2012 Christchurch earthquake damaged the Marmite factory, causing 'Marmageddon': a national Marmite shortage that made headlines and caused panic buying. Kiwi Marmite identity is deeply felt.

breakfast.name: Rewena Bread (Māori Potato Sourdough)
ingredients: Rewena (Māori potato sourdough starter — fermented potato and flour)
instructions: Rewena paraoa is leavened by a natural starter made from fermented potato water
The starter is called 'rewena' — maintained for generations in some families
Make the starter: boil and mash potato, cool, mix with flour, leave to ferment 2-3 days
The fermentation creates lactic acid — a mild, tangy flavor
Develop the dough, shape into a round
Bake in a camp oven (traditional) or conventional oven
The crust should be firm; the interior dense but soft
Rewena bread is the Māori traditional bread — made before European yeasted breads arrived
It represents Māori food sovereignty — adapting introduced potato into their own fermentation tradition
Shared at hui (Māori gatherings) and tangihanga (funerals)
breakfast.description: Māori potato sourdough — a naturally leavened bread using a starter (rewena) made from fermented potato water and flour, passed down through generations. The potato fermentation creates a mild tang and distinctive dense texture. Rewena bread represents Māori food sovereignty: taking an introduced crop (potato) and creating their own fermentation tradition. Made for hui and tangihanga.

breakfast.name: ANZAC Biscuits
instructions: Mix dry ingredients: oats, coconut, flour, sugar
Melt butter with golden syrup
Mix bicarbonate of soda with boiling water, add to butter mixture — it foams
Combine wet and dry ingredients
Roll into balls, flatten onto baking trays
Bake at 160°C — lower temperature for chewy biscuits (more time), higher for crispy
ANZAC biscuits were sent to soldiers by women during WW1
Made without eggs (eggs were scarce) — golden syrup and bicarb replaced the binding
They kept well in tin boxes on the long voyage to Gallipoli and France
ANZAC = Australian and New Zealand Army Corps
The biscuit is now protected under New Zealand law — it cannot be called ANZAC if it doesn't meet the traditional recipe
breakfast.description: New Zealand and Australia's WW1 commemorative biscuit — oats, desiccated coconut, and golden syrup baked without eggs (eggs were scarce; golden syrup and bicarb provided binding) into chewy-or-crispy biscuits. Made by women to send to soldiers at Gallipoli and the Western Front — they kept well in tins on the long ocean voyage. 'ANZAC' is legally protected in New Zealand.

breakfast.name: Feijoa and Yoghurt
ingredients: Feijoas (fresh — only available in autumn/winter, March-June in NZ)
instructions: Feijoa (Acca sellowiana) is a South American fruit completely adopted by New Zealand
It's the unofficial national fruit — every New Zealand backyard has a feijoa tree
Halve feijoas, scoop the flesh — the flesh is white, the skin is not eaten
The flavor: floral, aromatic, tropical, vaguely pineapple-guava with a hint of mint
Eating feijoas raw is the most common consumption
Serve scooped flesh over yoghurt with manuka honey
The glut: feijoa trees produce so prolifically that New Zealanders often have more than they can eat
Feijoa season (April-May) is a New Zealand cultural event — bags left at roadsides for free
Manuka honey is native New Zealand honey — from the manuka bush (Leptospermum scoparium)
breakfast.description: New Zealand's unofficial national fruit — feijoas (a South American fruit so enthusiastically adopted that every backyard seems to have a tree) scooped and served over yoghurt with manuka honey. The feijoa glut (April-May) is a cultural phenomenon: trees produce prolifically, neighbors leave bags on the street for free. The flavor is impossible to describe: floral, tropical, vaguely pineapple-guava with a mintiness.

lunch.name: Fish and Chips
ingredients: White fish (snapper, gurnard, or tarakihi — New Zealand species)
Batter: flour, beer (or sparkling water), salt
instructions: Fish and chips is New Zealand's most beloved takeaway — every small town has a fish and chip shop
Batter the fish: dip in seasoned flour, then beer batter
Deep fry the chips first — remove, let the oil come back to temperature
Deep fry the battered fish — 3-5 minutes per side
The batter should be golden and crispy, the fish inside moist
Chips should be thick-cut and soft inside
Wrap in paper (traditionally newspaper — now food-safe paper)
Eat at the beach, at a park, in the car
Salt and vinegar are the only condiments needed
The Friday fish and chip tradition: families ordering takeaway every Friday night
Snapper is the prestige New Zealand fish — mild, white, beautiful in batter
lunch.description: New Zealand's most beloved takeaway — snapper (New Zealand's prestige white fish) in beer batter with thick chips, wrapped in paper and eaten outdoors. Every small town has a fish and chip shop. The Friday night fish and chip tradition (families ordering takeaway) is woven into New Zealand family life. Eaten at the beach, the park, in the car.

lunch.name: Whitebait Fritters
ingredients: Whitebait (fresh — tiny juvenile fish, transparent, the whole fish is eaten)
instructions: New Zealand whitebait is the juvenile of 5 native galaxiid fish species
The whole fish is eaten — transparent, tiny, no need to clean
Whitebait season is a New Zealand cultural event: September-November
Mix whitebait gently with egg, salt, pepper — minimal handling
Cook in butter in a pan — thin fritters that set around the whitebait
They should be golden on both sides, the whitebait just cooked through
Whitebait fritters are served on white bread with a squeeze of lemon
The whitebait fills the fritter — not just flavoring
Premium whitebait can cost over NZ$100/kg — it's New Zealand's luxury food
Whitebait 'claims' on rivers — families return to the same spots generation after generation
The simplicity of the recipe is intentional — whitebait needs nothing
lunch.description: New Zealand's luxury seasonal fritter — transparent juvenile galaxiid fish (whole, unprocessed — the entire fish is eaten) bound with egg into thin fritters, cooked in butter. Whitebait season (September-November) is a cultural event; families hold 'claims' on the same river spots for generations. Whitebait can cost over NZ$100/kg. Served on white bread. The simplicity is intentional.

lunch.name: Boil-Up (Māori Pork Bone Soup)
ingredients: Pork bones (boil-up requires bone — the marrow and collagen are the point)
Dumplings (flour and water — cooked in the soup)
instructions: Boil pork bones in water — skim the foam
The long simmer (60-90 min) releases the marrow and creates a rich broth
Add kumara, potato, onion
Add puha (sowthistle) or watercress — it wilts in the hot broth
Drop flour-water dumplings into the simmering soup — they cook in 10-15 minutes
The dumplings are dense and stodgy — this is correct and desirable
Season with salt
Boil-up is the Māori comfort food and the dish of gatherings (hui)
Puha (sowthistle) is a common NZ weed that Māori adopted as a vegetable
The marrow from the bones is sucked out — it's the best part
Simple, nourishing, communal
lunch.description: Māori comfort food and gatherings dish — pork bones simmered until the marrow releases, with kumara (Māori sweet potato), puha (sowthistle — a New Zealand weed adopted as a vegetable), and flour dumplings cooked in the broth. Boil-up is the taste of hui (Māori gatherings) and tangi. The dense dumplings and rich marrow broth are the experience. Puha is the ingredient that makes it distinctly Māori.

lunch.name: Hāngī (Māori Earth Oven)
instructions: Hāngī is cooked in a pit dug in the earth — a method at least 700 years old in New Zealand
Light a large fire, heat stones to incandescent temperature — several hours
Dig the pit 60-90 cm deep
Lower the heated stones into the pit
Place baskets of food on top — meat on bottom, vegetables on top
Cover with wet cloths to create steam, then earth on top
Cook for 2-4 hours — the steam and heat cook everything simultaneously
The steam is trapped, creating a pressure-cooker effect
Uncover to a cloud of steam — the food is smoky, tender, moist
The earthy, smoky steam flavor is impossible to replicate in an oven
Hāngī is made for special occasions — tangi, weddings, celebrations, Waitangi Day
The community aspect is inseparable from the food — everyone helps
lunch.description: Māori earth oven — meat and vegetables loaded into wire or flax baskets, lowered onto incandescent stones in a pit, covered with wet cloths and earth, and steamed for hours. The trapped steam creates intense, smoky moisture that gives hāngī its unmistakable flavor — impossible to replicate with any other cooking method. Made for tangi, weddings, Waitangi Day. The community labor (digging, heating stones, lowering, uncovering) is inseparable from the meal.

lunch.name: Lamb Rack (New Zealand Spring Lamb)
ingredients: New Zealand lamb rack (frenched — 7-8 ribs per rack)
instructions: New Zealand spring lamb is arguably the world's best — pasture-raised, no feedlots
Press mustard and herb coating onto the meaty side
Roll in breadcrumbs mixed with rosemary and garlic
Sear fat-side down in a hot pan until golden
Roast at 200°C for 20-25 minutes — medium-rare to medium
Rest 10 minutes — essential for lamb, which tightens as it rests
Carve between the bones into individual cutlets
New Zealand produces 30 million sheep for 5 million people — 6 sheep per person
The pasture-fed, temperate-climate lamb has a sweet, clean flavor
New Zealand is the world's largest exporter of lamb
This is the flagship New Zealand luxury food — what the country is known for globally
lunch.description: New Zealand's flagship protein — spring lamb rack from the country that has 6 sheep per person, pasture-raised without feedlots in temperate grassland that produces the world's sweetest, cleanest lamb flavor. Herb-crusted (mustard, rosemary, breadcrumbs), seared, and roasted to medium-rare. New Zealand is the world's largest lamb exporter. The clean, sweet flavor of grass-fed New Zealand lamb has no equal.

dinner.name: Pavlova
instructions: The NZ vs Australia pavlova debate: both claim to have invented it in honor of Anna Pavlova (1920s)
New Zealanders believe a Wellington hotel invented it; Australians say Perth — unresolved
Beat cold egg whites to stiff peaks — the cold is important
Add caster sugar gradually — one tablespoon at a time
Fold in vinegar and cornflour — these create the marshmallow interior
The cornflour and vinegar are what distinguish pavlova from meringue
Spread into a circle on baking paper — high, domed shape
Bake at 120°C for 90 minutes, then LEAVE IN THE OVEN as it cools
The exterior should be crispy; the interior should be marshmallow-soft
The crack when cool is characteristic — not a failure
Top with whipped cream and fruit
Kiwifruit is the essential topping in New Zealand
dinner.description: The great Australasian dessert debate — New Zealand claims to have invented pavlova for Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova (as does Australia). The NZ version is characterized by cornflour and vinegar in the meringue, creating a crispy shell over a marshmallow interior. The crack as it cools is correct, not a failure. Topped with cream, kiwifruit, and passionfruit. The debate will never be resolved.

dinner.name: Kina on Toast (Sea Urchin)
ingredients: Kina (New Zealand sea urchin — Evechinus chloroticus)
instructions: Kina is the Māori name for the New Zealand sea urchin
Split the kina with a knife — a sharp rock can also do it
Scoop out the orange roe — this is what is eaten
The roe is creamy, intensely flavored — briny, ocean, slightly bitter
Eat immediately — the freshness is everything
Serve on buttered toast with a squeeze of lemon
Kina is polarizing — those who love it are passionate
The bitterness and intensity is what kina lovers seek
Kina is found on rocky coastlines throughout New Zealand
Māori have harvested kina for 700 years — coastal tradition
The season for the best kina roe: winter (June-August)
dinner.description: New Zealand's coastal delicacy — kina (native sea urchin) cracked open on the rocks, the creamy orange roe scooped onto buttered toast with a lemon squeeze. Kina is deeply polarizing: those who love its intense brininess and slight bitterness are passionate; others find it too strong. Māori have eaten kina for 700 years. Winter produces the most intensely flavored roe.

dinner.name: Pork and Puha (Māori)
instructions: Puha is a common weed in New Zealand that Māori adopted as a vegetable
Pre-European Māori had few vegetables — puha was important
Cook pork slowly in water until the fat renders and the meat falls from the bone
Add puha leaves in the last 20 minutes — it wilts into the broth
The bitter weed balances the rich fatty pork
Season minimally
Pork and puha is the simplest expression of Māori cooking — minimalism and respect for ingredients
The bitterness of puha against the richness of the pork is the flavor balance
Puha is available in New Zealand throughout the year — it's a 'weed'
This dish represents Māori adaptation: European pig + native weed = new tradition
Now considered a Māori comfort food classic
dinner.description: Māori minimalist cooking — slow-cooked pork (bone-in, fatty) with puha (sowthistle — a common New Zealand weed that Māori adopted as a vegetable). The dish represents Māori food adaptation: taking an introduced European animal (pig) and combining it with a native plant (puha). The bitter weed against the rich pork fat is the balance. Minimal seasoning — respect for the ingredients.

dinner.name: Green-Lipped Mussel Chowder
ingredients: Green-lipped mussels (Perna canaliculus — New Zealand's native mussel)
instructions: Green-lipped mussels are native to New Zealand — they exist nowhere else in the world
The green lip on the shell is the identifying feature
New Zealand farms 100,000+ tonnes per year — exported globally
Steam mussels open in white wine — reserve the liquid (it's the base of the chowder)
Make a roux, add milk and cream
Add the reserved mussel liquid, fish stock, potato
Cook potato through, add mussels back at the end (they're already cooked)
Season with parsley, salt, white pepper
Green-lipped mussels are larger and meatier than blue mussels
They contain omega-3 fatty acids — promoted as a health food
New Zealand mussel chowder is a coastal restaurant staple
dinner.description: New Zealand's endemic mussel in a cream chowder — green-lipped mussels (Perna canaliculus, native to New Zealand alone, farmed at over 100,000 tonnes per year) steamed open in white wine, the liquid becoming the chowder base with cream, potato, and fresh parsley. Green-lipped mussels are larger and meatier than European blue mussels. A New Zealand coastal restaurant staple.

dinner.name: Venison Casserole
ingredients: Venison (shoulder or leg — NZ farmed or wild)
instructions: New Zealand has 750,000+ wild deer — venison is abundant and free for hunters
Farmed venison is also a major export industry
Dust venison in seasoned flour — brown in hot oil in batches
The browning is essential — develops deep flavor
Fry onion, carrot, celery, garlic in butter
Add tomato paste, wine, stock, herbs
Return venison, cover, braise 90 minutes
The venison becomes extremely tender — it falls apart
Add mushrooms in the last 30 minutes
New Zealand venison is lean and clean-flavored — little gaminess compared to European venison
Serve with mashed potato or kumara
dinner.description: New Zealand venison braised in red wine — New Zealand has over 750,000 wild deer (red deer introduced for hunting in the 1800s), making venison abundant. The farmed venison export industry is also significant. New Zealand venison is notably lean and mild-flavored compared to European venison. Braised slowly with wine, root vegetables, and mushrooms until falling apart.

snacks.name: Hokey Pokey Ice Cream
instructions: Hokey pokey is the most popular ice cream flavor in New Zealand
The hokey pokey: sugar and golden syrup cooked to hard crack, bicarb added at the end to make it foam and aerate into honeycomb toffee
The honeycomb sets, is broken or crushed, and folded into vanilla ice cream
The result: vanilla ice cream with crunchy, caramel-sweet toffee pieces
The pieces soften slightly in the ice cream — between crunchy and chewy
Hokey pokey ice cream is available in every New Zealand supermarket and dairy (corner store)
The name 'hokey pokey' for honeycomb toffee is a New Zealand/Australian term
Tip top and Meadow Fresh are the dominant New Zealand ice cream brands
Kiwis often eat it from the block — no bowl
snacks.description: New Zealand's most popular ice cream flavor — vanilla ice cream with pieces of hokey pokey (aerated toffee honeycomb, made by adding bicarb to caramelized sugar and golden syrup). The honeycomb pieces soften slightly in the ice cream, giving a between-crunchy-and-chewy texture. Available in every supermarket and corner dairy. Often eaten straight from the block.

snacks.name: Lamington
ingredients: Sponge cake (baked in a square tin, cooled and cut)
Dark chocolate icing (melted chocolate + cream or water)
instructions: Lamingtons are shared between New Zealand and Australia (both claim them)
Square sponge cake, dipped in chocolate icing, rolled in desiccated coconut
The sponge must be a day old — fresh sponge tears when dipped
Dip each square in chocolate, let excess drip off
Roll immediately in desiccated coconut before the chocolate sets
The chocolate should thin enough to coat smoothly
The coconut sticks to the chocolate
New Zealand lamingtons sometimes have a cream and jam filling (variation)
Made for school fundraisers, morning teas, and Anzac Day
Part of the New Zealand 'morning tea' culture — the ritualized workplace tea break
snacks.description: New Zealand and Australia's shared sponge cake — day-old sponge squares dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut. The day-old sponge is essential (fresh sponge tears when dipped). New Zealand versions sometimes have a cream and jam filling. Made for school fundraisers and morning teas — part of New Zealand's strong workplace morning-tea culture.

snacks.name: Cheese Roll (South Island Specialty)
ingredients: Cream of mushroom soup (condensed — from a can)
instructions: The cheese roll is specific to the South Island of New Zealand — especially Otago and Southland
It is passionately championed by Southlanders as their regional contribution to New Zealand cuisine
Mix grated tasty cheese with condensed mushroom soup and onion soup mix
Spread generously on a slice of bread
Roll up tightly, place seam-side down
Grill or toast under the grill until golden
The cheese filling melts and becomes creamy
The outside should be crispy, the filling melty
The condensed mushroom soup is non-negotiable in the original South Island recipe
Cheese rolls are sold at service stations throughout the South Island
An unexpected and deeply loved regional specialty
snacks.description: The South Island's fiercely defended regional specialty — white bread rolled around a filling of grated cheddar, condensed mushroom soup, and onion soup mix, grilled until the outside crisps and the filling melts. Southlanders consider this their contribution to New Zealand cuisine. The condensed soup is essential — the canned soup is not a shortcut, it is the recipe. Sold at South Island service stations.

snacks.name: Tim Tam Slam
ingredients: Tim Tams (chocolate biscuits — an Australian brand beloved in NZ)
instructions: Tim Tams are an Australian chocolate biscuit beloved across New Zealand — sold in every supermarket
The Tim Tam Slam: a distinctly New Zealand and Australian way of eating them
Bite off a small piece from opposite corners of the Tim Tam
Use it as a straw to sip hot coffee or hot chocolate
The hot liquid melts the chocolate interior
You have about 3-4 seconds before the biscuit collapses entirely
Eat the whole biscuit immediately before it falls apart
The Tim Tam Slam requires timing and the correct angle
It is a rite of passage for anyone living in New Zealand or Australia
Introduced to international visitors as a cultural experience
The Slam is more famous abroad than the biscuit itself
snacks.description: New Zealand and Australia's shared chocolate biscuit ritual — a Tim Tam (chocolate-coated biscuit with chocolate cream filling) used as a straw for hot coffee by biting off opposite corners, sucking the liquid through, then eating the melting biscuit before it collapses. You have 3-4 seconds. The Tim Tam Slam is a cultural initiation for visitors and is performed with great ceremony.

desserts.name: Pavlova (see Dinner)
instructions: See dinner section for full recipe
The pavlova is New Zealand's national dessert — contested with Australia
The kiwifruit topping is the New Zealand signature
desserts.description: New Zealand's most iconic dessert — see dinner section for the full recipe. The combination of crispy meringue shell with marshmallow interior, topped with cream and kiwifruit, is New Zealand's national dessert (contested with Australia).

desserts.name: Afghan Biscuits
instructions: Afghan biscuits appear in the Edmonds Cookbook — New Zealand's most beloved cookbook since 1908
The Edmonds Cookery Book is in more New Zealand kitchens than any other book
Beat butter and sugar until creamy
Add flour and cocoa — the mixture is crumbly
Fold in cornflakes — they provide the signature crunch
Roll into balls, flatten slightly
Bake at 180°C for 15 minutes
Ice with dark chocolate icing while still warm
Top each with a walnut half — this is mandatory
The cornflake texture survives the baking — crunchy in a soft, chocolatey biscuit
The name 'Afghan' is mysterious — no connection to Afghanistan is documented
They are uniquely New Zealand
desserts.description: New Zealand's most beloved biscuit from the Edmonds Cookery Book (in more NZ kitchens than any other cookbook since 1908) — chocolate-cocoa dough with cornflakes for crunch, iced with dark chocolate, each topped with a walnut half. The name has no documented connection to Afghanistan. Afghan biscuits are New Zealand's most recognizable homemade biscuit.

desserts.name: Kiwi Pavlova Roulade
ingredients: Egg whites, caster sugar, cornflour, vinegar
instructions: A variation on the pavlova — the meringue baked flat and rolled
Line a Swiss roll tin with baking paper
Spread meringue mixture flat — 1cm thick
Bake at 180°C for 15 minutes — shorter time, higher heat than a full pavlova
Turn out immediately onto icing sugar-dusted baking paper
Roll while still warm — the meringue is flexible when hot
Cool, then unroll gently
Fill with whipped cream and sliced kiwifruit
Roll up again — the cracks on the outside are characteristic and expected
The roulade format makes pavlova easier to slice and serve at parties
The interior is the same marshmallow-soft meringue
desserts.description: The pavlova in roll form — meringue baked flat, rolled while hot (the cracks on the outside are expected), filled with whipped cream and kiwifruit. The roulade format makes the notoriously difficult-to-slice pavlova practical for parties. The interior maintains the same marshmallow softness as a traditional pavlova.

drinks.name: Flat White (Coffee)
ingredients: Steamed whole milk (micro-foamed — silky, not frothy)
instructions: The flat white is a New Zealand (and Australian) invention — the origin is contested but earnestly debated
New Zealand claims a Wellington café invented it in the 1980s
Australia claims Melbourne invented it simultaneously
The flat white: smaller than a latte, less foam, higher coffee-to-milk ratio
Steamed milk should be silky-smooth, glossy, no big bubbles — 'micro-foam'
Pour over the double espresso
Served in a smaller cup (150-180ml) than a latte (240ml)
The flat white demonstrates more espresso flavor than a latte
New Zealand's café culture is among the world's best — independent cafés dominate
Starbucks famously failed in New Zealand and Australia — closed most stores — because the local café culture was too strong
drinks.description: New Zealand and Australia's contested coffee creation — a double espresso with silky micro-foamed milk, smaller and stronger than a latte, in a 150-180ml cup. Wellington claims to have invented it in the 1980s; Melbourne disagrees. The flat white demonstrates that New Zealand's independent café culture is so strong it drove Starbucks to close most of its New Zealand and Australian stores.

drinks.name: L&P (Lemon and Paeroa)
ingredients: L&P is a commercially bottled soft drink — not homemade
instructions: L&P (Lemon and Paeroa) is New Zealand's own soft drink since 1907
Named after the natural mineral water from Paeroa (a town in the Waikato)
Originally: lemon juice mixed with the mineral spring water from Paeroa
Now: commercially bottled by Coca-Cola New Zealand
The slogan: 'World Famous in New Zealand' — self-aware and beloved
Lemon-citrus flavor, mildly carbonated, slightly sweet
L&P is found at every New Zealand event, barbecue, and dairy
The giant L&P bottle in Paeroa town is a tourist photo stop
The 'World Famous in New Zealand' slogan is an honest admission that no one outside NZ knows it
L&P is a quiet pride: New Zealand's own thing, for New Zealand
drinks.description: New Zealand's own soft drink since 1907 — lemon juice originally mixed with the natural mineral water from Paeroa springs, now commercially bottled. The slogan 'World Famous in New Zealand' is a self-aware, beloved acknowledgment that the drink has no international recognition. Found at every New Zealand barbecue and event. The giant L&P bottle in Paeroa is a tourist destination.

drinks.name: Manuka Honey Tea
ingredients: Manuka honey (Leptospermum scoparium — NZ native bush honey)
instructions: Manuka honey comes from bees that pollinate the native New Zealand manuka bush
UMF (Unique Manuka Factor) rating system — the higher the UMF, the more antibacterial activity
MGO (methylglyoxal) is the active compound responsible for the antibacterial properties
Manuka honey is among the world's most expensive honeys — NZ exports ~2000 tonnes/year
The flavor: earthy, slightly herbal, medicinal — more complex than clover honey
Stir into hot water — do NOT boil manuka honey (it destroys the active compounds)
Add lemon if desired
Manuka honey is taken for sore throats, wound care, and digestive health
Used in hospitals (as medical-grade dressings) and homes alike
The New Zealand manuka bush blooms for only 2-6 weeks per year — limiting supply
drinks.description: New Zealand's medicinal honey in its simplest form — manuka honey (from bees pollinating the native Leptospermum scoparium bush, blooming only 2-6 weeks per year) dissolved in hot water. The UMF/MGO rating measures antibacterial activity; medical-grade manuka is used in hospital wound dressings. Earthy, herbal, more complex than clover honey. The world's most expensive honey by volume.
